utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We are told there is a delay with the witness arriving, no doubt because of the weather, but we are also informed that counsel may wish to raise some matters with us, so we thought we would use the time for that purpose. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning. Your Honour, we have some housekeeping matters which we'd like to raise, and one concerns next week. We will have the psychiatrist here next week, and we know the Court wants a report as soon as possible, so we thought the key thing which would enable a report to come out within the next few weeks is to get the examinations completed. The doctors would like not only an examination, but they also want to videotape the examinations. We contacted the prison -- or I'm sorry, the detention facility, who indicates that that can be done but the hours are very limited. Our other option is doing it in the building. The Registry then raised the issue if we have a day of court and then the defendant -- I'm sorry, the defendant or the accused then eats, by the time we could start the interview it would be close to 3.00. What we would like to do is either have one day off, which would be take Tuesday off -- if we could take Tuesday off, we could get most of the examination done, possibly even one day - maybe Wednesday - shorter hours, but we would know after Tuesday how much could be completed. Now, normally we would feel that that would seriously affect the schedule of witnesses. We have a problem for next week. Ambassador Fietelaars, who was supposed to be our witness for Monday and Tuesday, had to return home for some personal matters. We do not have Ambassador Fietelaars for next week. As a result, we have -- we will finish this witness, then go into Mrs. Ogresta. Mrs. Ogresta we thought would go into Monday. Our next witness isn't even arriving until the weekend or Monday so we could barely put him on Tuesday, if not even place him on the witness stand on Wednesday. As a result, we have a very, very limited number of witnesses for next week. We have lost two days worth of witnesses. Taking one day off would not affect our schedule. It would enable the report -- or the examination to be completed and the report to be in as soon as possible. It would allow them to videotape the examination, and it should not have any affect on the case from the Prosecution's point of view. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, the prospect that you put to us of interrupting the hearing simply to make it more convenient for the medical examination has a familiar ring. It is exactly the position which the Defence wanted and which we were reluctant to accommodate, if I remember, and in the end, we indicated that we would start late - we were sitting in the afternoons at the time - but we would not allow them a full day. But you want now to have a full day for your own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. And there's two reasons. Number one, as you recall, at that time we had scheduling problems. Due to the loss of a few days, we had witnesses backed up. We were even sending witnesses that were here back home. We were flying them back. Next week we have a problem. We do not have sufficient witnesses. Even without losing a day for examination, we will probably have a day and possibly even more than a day where we have no witnesses, and we have to come before the Court and say because of losing Ambassador Fietelaars we do not have a witness. That's number one. Number two, when they made the request, they did not indicate it was a psychiatric examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, they did, in my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. They said a medical examination that would take seven hours. They never said psychiatric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But it was by a specialist psychiatrist. I would put two and two together there and make four.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At the time all we knew was a medical examination. It's not in the record that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, that's stretching, yes. But perhaps your strongest submission would be to have a day off on Tuesday because you simply have run out of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That is -- in all likelihood we will not have a witness anyway on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in connection with what Mr. Weiner is saying that has to do with the schedule of witnesses, the Defence has no position. In fact, it is at the discretion of you, Your Honour, and of course the Prosecutor how they feel this should be done. But this morning the Defence heard another thing which causes serious concern of the Defence which is the videotaping of a psychiatric finding is something that the defendant and the Defence will not agree to. This is the first time that we hear that someone is planning to film a psychiatric examination. In my career, which may not be all that long, I have never had occasion to hear of a similar practice. But in view of the situation and irrespective of that, the Defence and the defendant absolutely will not consent to that. I do not see a single purpose, a single reason why professional examiners would film on videotape their examination. This is something which so blatantly encroaches upon the privacy of the client and then can so blatantly be reflected on the content of what the psychiatric examination will be that this simply causes us serious concern and is something that the defendant and the Defence do not consent to. This is something that we hear for the first time this morning. This is something which is totally out of the ordinary and something which is wholly unnecessary. So please, Your Honour, take this into consideration also when making your decision as to how much time is necessary and what manner of organisation is required for the arrangements to be made for this medical examination and expert opinion on the part of the psychiatrist, but to film this on videotape, that is really totally unnecessary. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, the first question is the necessity -- the first question is the necessity of videotaping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, this is not my request. This is the request of the doctors. It is their practice. Some of the doctors in the United States take the practice that they videotape. Not only do they make their own notes during the examination, but they then take the tapes back and they watch it where they have a chance to sit and review the session after and to see whatever else they pick up and to make sure they didn't miss anything. They also review it with a team, their own team, to make sure that there is nothing that's missed. That is their practice. It's not a situation where the videotapes are turned over to the Prosecutors or it's anything we're requesting. This is their -- this is the process that they use. Also, where we have different doctors involved, they can contact each other. We have one doctor from Croatia, we have two doctors from the United States; one is from the West Coast, one is from Hawaii. They can contact each other, they can refer to different times, different periods, different actions, different matters or instance that they've seen and discuss it. That's why they use that type of technique. They're comfortable with it and they've made the request. What we want to do is use a room similar to this where you have videotape equipment. They have them at the detention facility and they have them at this building. We're not going to have someone walking around with a camera such as in a movie, taking pictures of the defendant Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. while -- with a video camera while the interview or the examination is occurring. This is a medical process. This is the type of process that they use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic, you heard some further development of the -- of the reason why the doctors, for their purposes, apparently would prefer to use a tape. Do you have any further submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I unfortunately have nothing to add to what I have already said. General Strugar does not consent to being videotaped during the psychiatric interview. This interview, as well as all other materials which are the result of the psychiatric analysis will be submitted to the parties. They can also be inspected and examined in this court and in all other ways. So this is totally unnecessary. This process that Mr. Weiner is referring to is being conducted in a room which is intended for interviews with the accused. So this will have all the implications that the room is, in terms of the views of the defendant and the people who are with him, it will have all the implications of an interview being given to the Prosecution. It is hard to distinguish in such circumstances what is a psychiatric need and what is the giving of an interview. And as I've already said, additionally, this grossly encroaches upon the privacy of Mr. Strugar. And as I've already mentioned, this has never been mentioned so far even though we've been discussing this examination for over a month now. So it is with regret that I have to repeat, Your Honour, that the accused Defendant Strugar does not agree to his psychiatric examination being taped. No one, Your Honour, since medical evaluations have been undertaken in the -- in this institution, no one has been videotaped during such examinations. Why should General Strugar be the first exception? For what particular reason? And many such examinations have been undertaken by physicians from America, from Serbia, from Croatia, from Europe, from all over the world, from all continents. So I don't see a problem in that. And as for the problems between Hawaii and the East Coast, that is something which neither General Strugar nor the Defence are concerned with. These people will be properly handsomely paid for their work and they need to devote appropriate time to their duty, look at this man, and render their opinion. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would point out, Mr. Petrovic, that it is your client who is raising the issue of his fitness to plead. It's not a matter of just an uninvited intrusion into his privacy. The medical experts that are being retained by the Prosecution, but they are independent experts, have indicated a preference to use this because it enables them not only to observe during the interview but to consider again after the interview in case they have missed something during the interview, so that it would seem on that basis that there could be some medical advantage for them in being able to consider the tape afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- I apologise. Just one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to repeat yet once again what I already said. First of all, there is a host of quandaries, of unknowns in this entire thing. First of all, we don't know who these people are. Of course we have confidence that these are adequately qualified people who will do their job properly. Secondly, it is not clear from what I heard what particular profile, what particular profile of this particular profession they are. Thirdly, I did not get it whether all these people would be coming here or one would come here and then videotape the examination and then send it to Hawaii. All these things are not clear to me, Your Honour. Secondly, if someone wishes to view something several times, to check and re-check, he can have it audiotaped. He can record it. He can jot it down, the way our experts have been doing. He can stay here for a day, two or three or five days more to test his impressions, to again broach -- raise a subject with the defendant, to analyse things that he finds need clarification. Please, Your Honour, it is quite true what you have said, that this is a request raised by the Defence. It is true that this is a problem because, according to Dr. Letic's finding, this is a man who is unfit to stand trial, but it is equally true that this precedent which they wish to set in this Detention Unit is something that we never had before. Of course this can be easily verified from medical findings. These are, of course, confidential matters, but they can be looked into. Not a single interviewee for this purpose has been videotaped. So I ask you kindly, Your Honour, not to allow General Strugar to become a precedent, especially not in a situation when we have been waiting for weeks, practically months now, for these esteemed experts to come, and now we are faced with this kind of a request with just one of them wanting to come and send videotapes to the other ones. Perhaps this is not the case. I will allow that possibility. But at any rate, this position is such, and please take it into consideration and take note of this position of ours, namely it can be audiotaped. Let that be a compromise. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Is there anything further, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, just as a point of clarification: All three doctors will be here. All three will examine the accused. All three -- or the two Americans would like the videotape. They are consulting with the third doctor, the Croatian. They will all three have access to the videos, to review them, or they would like to have access to the videos to review them to make sure there's nothing they've missed, to see if there's anything they would like to add so they get a full, complete picture of what occurred. You get a complete picture by looking after, by listening again, and hopefully they can get the best diagnosis that they're able to get by getting the full picture. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it that you do not dispute what is put by Mr. Petrovic, that this would be the first time that that process has been followed in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In this Tribunal but this is probably the first time we've had a competency hearing as to psychiatric fitness in this Tribunal too. So we've barely had this situation raised other than one or two defendants just examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, the second issue, Mr. Weiner. You mentioned Tuesday. Bearing in mind the interests of Defence counsel, would Monday be as convenient to you and the witnesses? I mean the witnesses rather than you, that is the medical experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, because they're flying in Sunday and some are arriving Monday morning, so they were hoping to all have a full meeting. Some are meeting -- two are going to meet, I believe, on Sunday, and one is going to meet -- the three are going to meet Monday afternoon. So we're hoping for Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was trying to secure a long weekend for the Defence but it doesn't seem that it will fit for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are of the view that the unavailability of witnesses for Tuesday provides a reason to agree to the Prosecution request that there be no hearing on that day, that happening to make it more convenient for the medical examinations that are to be conducted. Were it not for the unavailability of other witnesses, we would not have been minded to treat the Prosecution request differently from the earlier request we had from the Defence of a similar nature. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. We would, therefore, indicate that we will not sit on Tuesday of next week. With respect to the further request that this Chamber authorise the videotaping of the interview, we are not presently persuaded of the medical necessity for that. We can appreciate that it may have had some convenience for the medical specialists, especially as they will be -- have come from and will return to different parts of the world, but in view of the concern of the accused, his reluctance to be involved in a videotaped interview and the obvious potential for his concern in itself to affect his emotional composure if he is being videotaped, we think it better that we do not authorise the videotaping of the interviews. Was there any other matter that the Prosecution wished to raise at this moment, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I hope our witness is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any matter that Defence counsel needs to raise at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't apologise, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Yes, in the desire for us to make the best use of our time, to use it most efficiently, but it so happens that we do not have anything to raise. But unfortunately it will crop up eventually when we will have other things to deal with. That's the way it usually happens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the witness has arrived, we are told, and will be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vlasica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I could remind you of the affirmation you gave to tell the truth. It still applies. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vlasica.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you were shown that map. Can you take a look at it, sir. And you marked on the map where your store was on Od Puca Street.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is that mark still there?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is that the correct location?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to offer the map at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P13.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like the map marked P13.1 or should we give it just a full new number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have been using quite separate numbers in other cases, so I think we'll continue that practice, although I must say my own personal preference is exactly what the court officer has done, but we were counselled that it would be more useful for some purposes if it went the other way, so we'd better be consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So that will be P83.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that that's P83, please. It said P3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm thinking that -- is this the map that was marked for identification as 83 or a separate one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. We requested -- we offered it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I believe it should be 85.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think the document doesn't say for what I put in yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So I believe the correct number is now Exhibit P85. And I just want to be sure that it's not the same map that was marked for identification as 83.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The only reason I changed that is it first listed P3. Based on this situation, could we have the witness sign it at this point, just for protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was wrong in raising 83. It's a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've got ourselves clarified, and this is Exhibit P85, and the witness is now signing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a man by the name of Mato Skocko?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did he have a son?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was the son's name?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tonci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was that the same Tonci that you saw with the bread truck, driving past you on December 6 in the early morning hours between 6.30 and 7.00 with a little truck with bread on it?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's not really a truck, but it's a type of vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you learn from your friend that something happened to his son on December 6th?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning, I did not know. I found out only a few days later, in hospital, that the young man was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when did you learn that he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days later, in hospital. Perhaps two or three days later. Then I found out who all the people who were killed in the territory of the town of Dubrovnik were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry: On what date was he killed?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you learn how he had been killed, from the father?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I found out from the medical staff, from the nurses and doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they say what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did they say?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the shelling, some shrapnel from a shell, a small fragment, hit him at the door and went through the right side of his body directly into the heart. So they didn't even notice the entry wound because there was no blood. The young man turned around, and two metres further on he fell, dead. Afterwards, they carried out an autopsy in the hospital, and they realised that it was such a tiny fragment but that it did pierce the heart nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you talked about your injuries that you suffered on December 6th and that you were in the hospital for a little bit over two weeks. As a result of those injuries suffered, did you receive a disability from the government?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given the status of civilian invalid because I was not in the military of Croatia's, so I am being treated as a 30 per cent disabled person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you some papers at this time. Sir, I'd ask you to please look at the document with the ERN number 03517595 on it. It has a B as in "boy" in the upper right. It's a decision and it's the document with the stamp. Do you see that document, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you go to the second page of that. Now, there are a group of four statements at the top of the second page, and I'd like to read the second statement. It begins: "First Instance Medical Committee..." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "First Instance Medical Committee for the medical examination of the persons covered by the Law on the Protection of Military and Civilian War Invalids evaluated by its Finding and Advice number 141/96 from the 23rd of April, 1996, the invalidity of the above-mentioned at --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you slow down a little bit for the translators and stenographer, please. Could we continue with right after the date, 23 April, 1996, and just slowly read the rest.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... the invalidity of the above-mentioned at 30 per cent due to: condition after the wounding of the right upper leg with pronounced deformation of the muscle. T.309."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you go to the next document exhibit with the C on the top in the B/C/S. It's 03517597. I'm sorry. Could you go to the third document. I apologise. Strike that. 0517599 at the top without any letter. The third document of this set. It says "Finding and Opinion," in B/C/S. Do you see that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there are, under "Finding and Opinion," there are four statements. Could you read what's typed in under the first statement where it starts, "The condition after the wounding ..." Could you read that in for the record, please, under 1.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The condition after the wounding of the right upper leg with pronounced muscle deformation T.309."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to offer these three documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want anything to come into evidence with respect to the third of them or just simply to be accepted as it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, just to be accepted with it because that is the full three-part set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence is opposed to having a number assigned to this document right now for the same reason that we stated in respect to the first document. We have our reasons for that. We want the Defence to deal with it, but we are not opposed to having it marked for identification. As for the third document, the Prosecutor has to be aware of the fact that it is totally illegible, and that is why he probably withdrew it, because the witness could not have read it in the first place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a document, Mr. Rodic, that you have not had notice of, or these documents ones you have not had notice of?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all three documents were submitted to the Defence last night at 6.00 p.m. I think that no further comment is required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That being the case, Mr. Weiner, I think as a matter of courtesy we will defer until the closing of the cross-examination and your re-examination whether to receive the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fair. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As long as you remember to remind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it seems that a copy that Mr. Rodic has may not be legible. No doubt between you you can resolve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Do you want this document to come under one number or separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You could do it one number A, B, C or 1, 2, 3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, so that will be P86.1, .2, .3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: For identification at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document ending in 595 will be .1. The document ending in 599 will be .2, and the document ending in 597 will be .3. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we'll finish up. Did you eventually become a member of the military?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When did you join the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what sort of function did you have in the Croatian military in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drove a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in that military?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, let's go back to October, November, December 1991. Did you ever see any sort of artillery weaponry in the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any mortars in the Old Town of Dubrovnik in that same time period, October?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any anti-aircraft guns or any sort of anti-aircraft or smaller -- smaller artillery pieces in the Old Town in October, November, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever observe any outgoing fire from the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any soldiers up on the walls or the ramparts in the Old Town of Dubrovnik from October through December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please ask the witness to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, did you ever see numbers of Croatian soldiers in the Old Town in October through December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vlasica. I'm Goran Rodic, attorney-at-law from Podgorica, and on behalf of General Strugar's defence, I'm going to put a few questions to you in relation to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since we speak a similar language and since we understand each other and due to interpretation-related problems, we should not overlap each other. Please wait for me to put my question and then give your answer.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, during 1991, you lived in Klisevska Street number 13, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which is at Babin Kuk; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that near your house there were hotels at that time, Zagreb, Kompas?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, near my house, yes. Not very nearby, but around there. Zagreb about 200 metres, Kompas about 3 or 400 metres, towards the bay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is this the first time that you're in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When did you come?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You arrived in the morning; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You never came to The Hague before in relation to any kind of obligations vis-a-vis the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who else came to The Hague together with you from Dubrovnik, people from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some people came, but who it was, I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone here?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was just told that some individuals were here, but I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So during these five days you've been on your own. You didn't see any other people from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I've been all on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to see Djelo Jusic?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Nikola Jovic?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know them?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you bring your medical documentation with you when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you ever submit this documentation to the OTP before you came here?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What were all the documents that you brought along and what did you give to the Prosecutor specifically?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So altogether, these four documents.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have any other documents on you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have the originals of these documents here with you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have them right here, now?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They're at the hotel, the safe at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed the school for salespeople, a three-year secondary school, and after that I did my military service and then I trained for another two years in order to be trained as head of a shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, this was before you went to the army, I mean this additional training?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said it very nicely. Later, after, I did my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What a pity. We speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the period from 1979 until today, have you ever had a criminal record?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Or were any proceedings instituted against you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The company Dubrovkinja, where you worked during 1991, was a socially owned or state-owned company, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A state-owned company, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since when have you had a private shop?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This is the shop in Mlini that was referred to?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I worked in Mokosica for five years, and then I closed that shop and opened a new one in Mlini.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that your own shop? Do you own the premises?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I rented the space.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have anything like that in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you make any statements to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this on the 30th of May, 2000, in Dubrovnik, and was Dirk Hooijkaas the investigator who talked to you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it did take place then, but I don't know the gentleman's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- do you remember Andrea Bralic who did the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was a girl there, but I don't remember her exact name either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you tell the investigator everything that you considered to be of relevance?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same things I am saying now I said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, have you read this statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have because it was English and I don't speak English. But later on, when they translated it, then I read that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when it was later that you were given this version in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had another meeting with them, and then they brought it to me and they asked me to confirm what I had said, and I said that all of it was correct and that what was written down was exactly what I had said, and that is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this other meeting you had with them, how much time had gone by between those two interviews?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a year. I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you were given the version of your statement in the Croatian language after a year, which you then read and signed the English version; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it was, because I could see that it was -- that it reflected exactly what I had said, but I did not sign the English version but the Croatian version. Of course, I cannot read English, and I had to sign what was written in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the 30th of May, 2000, after you completed this interview in which participated the investigator and the lady translator, were you read out at that time the statement compiled in English, and did the lady interpreter interpret it for you into Croatian to see what was written?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was a different date. I cannot recall the exact date. Don't try to trip me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to trip you. What it says is this date, the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course they read what I had said and they read it out to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: They read it out to you in English or was it translated to you into Croatian?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And after a year, they gave you this written statement translated into Croatian in writing which you then read and signed?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After it had been written, yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you give the investigators the medical documentation in the year 2000 when they came to see you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me why you didn't give it to them?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because nobody asked me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you mention to them that you had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally they already knew everything, just like you now know everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So on that occasion, the investigator didn't ask you to hand over any documentation at all?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, I cannot tell you exactly. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was it exactly that asked this documentation from you and when?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was The Hague Tribunal. They told me that I should bring it along when I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So on the 22nd of February you arrived at The Hague. So can you tell me, in relation to the 22nd of February, how long before that was it that they had asked you to submit - i.e. bring - this documentation?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was about a month before that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did they mention, when they asked you this a month before that date, that you should send it by fax or similar ways?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but as I had no possibilities and I had a lot of choice -- a lot of work to do with my business, I didn't. And it was also hard to gather all the documents. I went to the hospital. It was hard to collect all the documentation, because 13 years had elapsed after also. So I really had great difficulty. They had great difficulty to find the document for me. That's for one document. For the other documents which you are seeing now, those I already had, but of course I wanted to compile a complete file of documentation in order to bring a proper file here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you talked to the investigators in the year 2000, and the year after that, in the year 2001, you were given the statement in Croatian for you to read and sign. So tell me, from that time up to date, have you had occasion, and if so, where and when, to re-read your statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you can see for yourself --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear counsel because of the overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see these documents which I have before me, which you have, are documents which I had been given a long time ago, so I put together this documentation, and that is I did my best. There is no reason for me to remember any bad things.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you didn't understand me quite correctly.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is from the year 2001 to this day, have you had occasion to re-read your statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did anyone read out your statement to you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the year 2001 when I received it and signed it. Actually, after that I was no longer interested in it. This is what I said, and I stand behind my words, and I have no reason to be concerned with that any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you read it now in The Hague after you came here?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the record should reveal an indication of Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there any mistakes in the statement which you read?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything reflected exactly my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So what you said in the statement is what you're saying today in court.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: There was no need for any corrections.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, I assume that after having served the military, you were assigned in accordance with the law on the military obligation into the reserve force of the JNA, were you not?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me to what particular unit.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Territorial Defence Reconnaissance Unit. I was a reconnaissance soldier according to establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you kept this establishment post also in the reserve?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this Territorial Defence unit, who did it belong to? Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was within the framework, I believe as would it be only normal, of Trebinje, because we were to Trebinje, to Duz for training, and to this location -- help me. If you can help me remember the name. It's in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter. I suppose then that you did military exercises as part of the Trebinje Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In 1991, you were 34 years old, and you were still a military conscript. You were still eligible for the draft?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was, but I was not a military conscript any more because I finished that in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what it was that you finished?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reserve formation. Namely, I was given a document to the effect that I was no longer a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in all fairness I really don't know. Perhaps because of the volume of my work or because I had put on some weight. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So at 34, the army could do without you. That is quite unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but it was a commonly known fact why I was excluded, because people knew what lay in store in the -- what would happen over the next two or three years, and the entire Territorial Defence of Dubrovnik was dismantled and all the weapons were taken to the Trebinje barracks so that we were left without weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You are referring to 1989 [1999] when they sort of wrote you off from the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes exactly, because they knew exactly what was going to happen. In fact, they had been planning beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour. I don't want to object, it's just the transcript says you're referring to 1999. Should that be corrected?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It should be 1989. That was the question I think you asked, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you explain in more specific terms what was it was that was being planned as of 1989? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was being planned? This is something that the top brass of the Yugoslav People's Army knows or knew, and the Yugoslav leadership, because if they had withdrawn the complete armaments of the Territorial Defence, that we in the city of Dubrovnik could no longer have any weapons, it only meant that this was being done in a planned fashion. Now, what was being planned? I think you know that better than anybody else. What was being planned was what happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have any prejudices vis-a-vis my person or --

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Because you say I knew, I know what was -- what had been in store, what was being planned.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because you are the Defence counsel for this gentleman. Of course I have respect for you, but I -- this is the way I have to say it. How else could I put it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But when you say that they dismissed you from the reserve force in 1989 and you only stopped being a member of the League of Communists only in 1990, that is a bit illogical, don't you think?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look here, I'll tell you this: Had I known what would happen, I would have perhaps left the League of Communists even earlier, but I think that it is not at all important at this point when I ceased being a member of the League of Communists because this is really immaterial vis-a-vis this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you believe it unimportant?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do. I think it unimportant because it is something else that we are now discussing. We are not discussing what I was and whether I was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But our distinguished colleague the Prosecutor asked you before I did. It was not me who started asking you this question.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But you replied to him.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I did. I had to tell him my entire biography because he has to have all these particulars. So, of course, do you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to also give me all the replies I want. I want --

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I will tell you everything that I want -- that you want to hear and that I know the answer to. Of course I will be telling you the truth, except when I don't know I will not reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was the rank that you had when you left the army?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was lance corporal. When I left the reserves. I apologise. I didn't quite get your question. When I left the reserves I was given the rank of Second Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And in this period since you finished serving the military service up to 1989, what was your promotion record? How come and on what basis?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I went for training twice and because of my merits.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What training?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Makarska for training of reconnaissance and sabotage units two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say on the basis your merits, that means that you were, so to speak, a good soldier also in the reserve and gave a good account of yourself?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And were you maintaining -- was your name in the military department, in the recruitment office in Dubrovnik records?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did the recruitment office in Dubrovnik actually exclude you from the reserve?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since so many years have elapsed, I am not sure, but I'm quite sure this instruction came from the top, but from where exactly, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "from the top"?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the top echelons of the Yugoslav People's Army. It couldn't have been anyone from the centre of the city unless such instructions have been passed down from some people who were to remove us, so to speak, from the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. During the break, in contact with the Victims and Witness Unit, I was asked about another one of the Prosecution witnesses about to come, and that is Ivo Vujnovic, Your Honour. I don't know whether we should deal with this matter in front of this witness or should the witness be asked to wait before we resolve the matter that has to do with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does it directly concern his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the witness could stay seated. If you'll excuse us. Just stay where you are and we'll deal with another matter. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness Ivo Vujnovic was announced by the Prosecution in its submission on the 25th of February, and it was stated that he would testify on the 2nd of March. So again the seven-day deadline was not observed, and this is what had been established at the Pre-Trial Conference on the 15th of December, last year. That is one point. Another thing is far more of a problem and it has to do with the testimony of that witness. Part of the material for him, namely transcripts, was disclosed to the Defence only two days ago, and it was only last night that the Defence received audiotapes. The point of these transcripts and the audiotapes is that intercepts, alleged intercepts were recorded pertaining to the 6th of December, 1991, and this was done by the mentioned witness. Bearing in mind the disclosure order between the parties which cannot be less than ten days, and that was also established at the pre-trial conference on the 15th of December last year, the Defence indeed is not in a position to prepare itself to cross-examine this witness. During such a short period of time, we cannot deal with all this material. Therefore, it would be useful if this witness were not brought to The Hague at that point in time so that no undue expenses are incurred by way of his travel and so on. It would be better if he could come on another occasion and testify then so that he could be dealt with during one trip. So this material is the core of the matter that his testimony deals with, and we are not in a position to check it out during such a short period of time. We cannot listen to the intercept. We cannot consult experts in this particular field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are these intercepts military intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And they relate to the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The -- it is true the tapes themselves were disclosed, as I found out, I think, two days ago. The Prosecution, we understood that they had been disclosed some time ago. It seems to have been an administrative oversight not to have disclosed the tapes themselves. We certainly disclosed the transcripts of the tapes within the required time period under the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The exact date? Can I just consult with the case manager? My learned friend's submission has taken me just by surprise at this particular time. The 24th -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of February, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And how extensive are these transcripts and tapes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From memory, I think there's about 15 pages of transcripts. That's from memory. My learned friend can correct me if I'm wrong. The -- it would have been well within time had Mr. Fietelaars, Ambassador Fietelaars testified as anticipated next week. We weren't anticipating Mr. Vujnovic testifying until sometime later next week, and we had to reschedule him because Mr. Fietelaars became unavailable due to personal reasons at the beginning of the week. The nature of the -- the nature of the evidence, it doesn't actually concern -- there certainly aren't intercepts involving the accused, orders, or anything directly from the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They must be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They're relevant as to the fact of an extent of communications between JNA units on the 6th of December, 1991. That's as far as the Prosecution will take the evidence of this witness. He was a person who was intercepting -- an amateur, so to speak, intercepting and taping conversations and then making transcripts of them and providing intelligence to the Croatian authorities. It -- that's the limit of it. It's only to establish the extent of and the fact of JNA communications on the 6th of December, which is circumstantially leading to circumstantial inferences available back up to the accused and the chain of command. So in that sense, it's -- the late disclosure is -- is not as prejudicial as it may seem at first blush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But there would have been no opportunity to have any technical evaluation of the tapes if they are not disclosed until two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course. The -- there is a difficulty with these tapes, and we will be relying more heavily upon the transcript and the fact of the witness identifying what was said by his transcript rather than the tapes. The tapes are very unclear. They're very - what's the word? - soft, hard to hear, and the witness has had to go back himself to transcribe them in Zagreb. We tried to transcribe them here but the interpreters couldn't do so so he's gone back to transcribe them himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That only strengthens the concern of Mr. Rodic, I would think, that they have adequate time with the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can't -- I don't -- of course the Prosecution doesn't disagree that the Defence, of course, should have proper preparation time if they want to cross-examine the veracity of the tapes and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re, let me indicate the Chamber's first impression; that is that it would be quite impractical to expect the Defence to cross-examine next week this witness. Whether you would want to call him in chief is a different matter, but as Mr. Rodic points out, it would be perhaps more efficient if the witness came at a later time and got his evidence and his cross-examination over at the one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could we possibly revisit this a little bit later in the day when I've -- when we've had a chance to speak to VWU and work out witnesses and -- and so? I certainly understand Your Honour's point. I'll be in a much better position to respond to it maybe in an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, there are two issues. The first is whether the Defence should be required to cross-examine the witness if the witness is called. I think you can take it the answer is no. For the Prosecution, then, will be the consequential question, whether to proceed with calling the evidence of this witness in chief or whether to have another witness, if one is available, or whether to have even more time not sitting. I leave that with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we will hear in due course. Mr. Rodic, we've rather moved ahead of you, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry that my learned friend Mr. Re is improvising now in your presence, although I gave you the exact figures. It is not true that we received the audiotape two days ago. We received it last night at 6.00 p.m. The transcripts were given to us two days ago. That is correct. The transcripts do not amount to 15 pages but a lot more. And another thing that is correct is that this witness, on the 15th of December last year, gave a statement to the investigators of the OTP and, at that time, he handed over these audiotapes and his transcripts. It's been more than two months since then. That is accurate information in relation to this submission put forth by the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You heard the position that was indicated to Mr. Re, Mr. Rodic. We leave it to the Prosecution whether or not they call the witness next week, but if they do, you will not be required to cross-examine, and that will have to happen at a later time. And as you suggest, it may be more practical to defer the witness altogether to a later time. So I think we can -- you can rest easy on that at the moment. It may be that the Prosecution will want to introduce a different witness at somewhat short notice. We'll have to see whether that produces any problems when and if that should happen. I think we can carry on now with the cross-examination of our very patient witness sitting here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, we will continue now with the cross-examination. I would be interested in the following: During 1990 and 1991, did you get any call-up papers from the military department?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was there any mobilisation in Croatia before October 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was general mobilisation declared in Croatia later?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about these last three months of 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you listen to the radio regularly?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear through the media that there was a general mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have a military booklet?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are your years of military service during the war registered in there?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the Yugoslav army or for the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I mean the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from 1993 until 1996, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And before you joined the Croatian army, can you tell me which formation you were in in the defence of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a civilian in the Civil Defence. It's not a formation. It's not part of the military establishment. It is there to help civilians; to put people in shelters, to bring food, to bring material that is indispensable for people who are in shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who was commander of the Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What position did you have in the Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a mere worker, believe me. Nothing. I mean, when some help was needed, then they called me to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does this Civil Defence have an establishment of its own with its own command, et cetera? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who was it that called you up then?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was people who were organised in this respect. I don't know whether there were any formations involved. I just know that they called me and said, "Ivo, this should be taken here and that should be taken there. Could you take this food to the shelter," things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said "at the level of the people who were involved in the organisation." Those were your exact words.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? What do you actually mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who were in charge of the Old Town so that it would function somehow, because there were a great many civilians in the Old Town. That is to say that things had to be organised so that these people could somehow live in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please focus on my question, and please give me brief and succinct answers because of the time limits involved. So you've been repeating time and again what the Civil Defence does. I know. We heard about that three times from you. I am asking you specifically how they got in touch with you as a member of the Civil Defence. Who was it that called you up? Who are these people who are organised at this level, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would receive a telephone call, and who these people are, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which telephone did they use? Where did they call you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called my number at the store.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And an unknown person phones you at the store and makes you go here and there in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that anybody made me go here and there. We were all involved because we were all supposed to help each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who these X, Y people are?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive such calls around midday or in the afternoon or in the early evening? Please wait for me to finish my question.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I still haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So was it necessary for you to provide your services for the Civil Defence during other times of the day; midday, afternoon, early evening?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So by when were all these needs of the population in Dubrovnik over in relation to your duties in the Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned myself, it was between 6.00 and 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So where did you spend your working hours between 6.00 and 8.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the store.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that your job before the war, too, to sell these food products at the store?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you do that same job between 6.00 and 8.00 in the morning while you were at the store in this period between October and December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When did you then carry out your activities related to the Civil Defence and assisting people in terms of material, bringing them food to the shelters, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was the head of that particular facility, of course I had my workers, my employees, and if anything was needed, then I took care of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, you told me that you spent the time between 6.00 and 8.00 in the morning at the workplace, in the shop. You did not mention that you left at any point.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't because it all depended on the needs involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who would call you and who would tell you about these needs? Could you please explain this to us. What was this all about?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a person whose name I would not know would phone me at the store and tell me, "Ivo, please take such-and-such an amount of bread and such-and-such an amount of water to a shelter," Ivo would do it and go back to the shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you remember any other task that you carried out on behalf of the Civilian Defence except for carrying milk?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the only thing I did. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you're a member of the Civilian Defence, and in terms of all of the activities in the October - December 1991 period, the only thing you did was go out a few times in the period between 6.00 and 8.00 a.m. in order to take some milk to the shelters.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you were the boss, if you were the foreman, why couldn't one of your workers take that milk there?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know how it was. If I -- I wouldn't have wanted a woman to go out and expose herself to risk. And I received that order, so I thought it was the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, are you personally ashamed or is there any other reason why you don't want to talk about your participation in the 1991 war?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My question is, are you perhaps ashamed or is there any other reason why you do not wish to explain to us here your participation in this period from October to December 1991 in the, shall I say, Civilian Defence of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no shame. I did what I did during the war. I'm proud of it. I did it to help the people, and I'm proud of having helped them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you helped these people on the orders of unknown people; right? Did you ever help any people without having received the orders from anyone?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, when the need arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were these needs daily needs?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the actual time. Of course, if someone was in need, I would see to that particular need of that particular person. I would help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your statement which you gave the investigators in the year 2000 in paragraph 2 you describe how the attack on Srdj had started on the 1st of October by shelling. Then in that paragraph, you say: "I noticed a number of smaller JNA patrol boats in the area. They would stay away at a safe distance so that shells could not hit them." Can you tell me what you meant by this, these boats were being away at a safe distance, maintaining a safe distance in order not to be hit by shells.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that these patrol boats which had blockaded Dubrovnik were a bit away from the walls. And as for the shells not hitting them, it could have been a stray shell that could have hit your own boat. That's what I meant, and that's what they sought to avoid.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: From my side, from where I'm standing, I cannot hit a single boat, Mr. Vlasica.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I meant from the side of the Yugoslav People's Army. I apologise to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So these patrol boats were a bit off at a safe distance from the ramparts of the Old Town in order to avoid getting hit by JNA shells?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I saw it. That's what I thought. We had no weapons, and this is the only thing I had in mind when I made the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who didn't have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
