utterances.text: Mr. Vlasica, don't you remember that yesterday you said that you saw the statue of St. Joseph hit when you were leaving the Old Town as you were being driven in this car? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I haven't finished. Do you remember then that you also saw Onofrio's fountain as being hit?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And you saw all this from the car?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was only normal. But if you take into consideration, if you think about it, one could see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why do you not make a single reference to this in your statement from 2000?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I told them what they asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And at hospital, were you -- did they give you a transfusion?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but how much blood I received, I really cannot recall. I only know that Dr. Bogdanovic told me, "Ivo, everything will be all right." And I know that the drip was by my side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let us please -- will you please shorten your answers.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you state the following on page 2, the penultimate paragraph, you say: "When I arrived at the hospital, they x-rayed my leg to see if the bone had been damaged. They subsequently gave me a blood transfusion and bandaged my leg up. After five or six days, they stitched up my wound." And you stayed in the hospital until the 21st of December, 1991. Is this, what you stated here, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you also remember whether you received any anti-tetanus shots or some antibiotics?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given some injections. I remember Dr. Mahanitoni [phoen] came every morning. They cleaned, of course, my wound, and it goes without saying that I did receive some injections in the thigh.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many of these injections you had to be given?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it more than five?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. How can you ask me these things? I can't recall such stupid things.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlasica, this is not stupid. This is your life we are talking about. You had bled profusely, so can you remember whether you were given one, three, five or ten shots during your treatment?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the while, all the time which I spent in hospital, I was already in a much better condition because I was -- first of all, I was relieved, personally, being in hospital, and I knew that I was surrounded by medical staff and that I would be helped. And believe me, they undertook -- they did everything they could to properly treat my wound and deal with it. And as I was otherwise generally healthy as I am now, I believe that this will --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlasica, I have to stop you. I have to interrupt you. You are very verbose. You said you received a shot in the thigh. Do you remember whether you received just that one injection that you remember or were there more?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were more, I'm sure, because they must have given me something against sepsis. I don't know what exactly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why don't you refer by a single word in your statement to the fact that you were actually clenching gauze between your teeth, that the nurse lay on top of you to hold down your arms and legs? Why don't you mention this by a single word about all these efforts that you had to suffer during the administration of medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because as I keep telling you, I only responded to questions that were being put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Vlasica, I have to ask you, who forged this document of the 18th of February, 2004, which confirms that you were treated from the 6th of December to the 21st of December at the general hospital in Dubrovnik? Do you know who falsified this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Falsified?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to know if the counsel has a good faith basis to make that claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, reading the content of this document, listening to the witness, and having seen other documentation, I absolutely have grounds to contend, to assert that this is a forgery, and what my learned colleague Weiner said yesterday in reference to the content of this document, I can say that this is an insult to common sense, because this document says: "On the basis of clinical findings, we establish that this is a tangential entry and exit wound of the left upper leg, rather more to the side, at the edge of the upper third, and there is profuse bleeding from the wound."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter doesn't have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you remember, yesterday when this piece of evidence was admitted, my learned colleague Weiner, on page 92, lines 5 and 6, in response to a question of yours, said to you: "Your Honour, this witness, when he came here, brought this document. It is in the process of translation. We can give it to the interpreters. I would like him to read it or shall we give it to the interpreters to interpret?" Already at that moment a document with an English translation was on the ELMO. At that point, the Witness Vlasica confirmed that this was his paper of discharge, and on page 93, row 15, you intervened, Your Honour, yesterday, and you pointed out for Colleague Weiner that it seemed from the translation that a different leg was being described than the other indicated by the witness. And what I say is an insult to common sense is on page 93, line 18, where Colleague Weiner says, in responding to you: "Yes, I know, but that is on their left and on his right if you look at him. That is from their aspect on the left side but with respect to this person it is on the right side." I presume, I assume, I am certain that he has explained to you how a physician looks at a patient and describes his findings. Also, I have lots of other objections to this particular document. First of all, the diagnosis. "Vulnus Explossivum Femoris Sin" has been miswritten. In the word "Exlossivum" there is a superfluous 'S'. The seal, the stamp on this document which says "Directrix" is unclear, but we can see from this copy that the "Directrix" has been typed over the stamp. So this means that the document was first stamped and then the word was typed over it. In the diagnosis, underneath the actual diagnosis is the prescribed therapy, where it says: "Treatment. Treatment --" and then it is followed by an English word. So we're talking about a document in the Serbian language where an English word is used. I'm spelling it out: D-R-A-I-N-A-G-E. It should be an 'E' instead of an 'A' if we want it to be correct even in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's also a French word, which may have a relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't heard, Your Honour, that they had been using French words or, rather, this one word when recording medical findings in Dubrovnik in 1991, or in Belgrade or Podgorica, for that matter. Also, the textual description of the wound does not correspond to the Latin diagnosis. So essentially, our objections are the grounds from which I actually derive what is my basic contention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, thank you for that. I think we've dealt with two matters at once; firstly the grounds upon which you would submit in the end that the document is a forgery; and secondly, the basis upon which you believe you may properly put to the witness that it is a forgery. I think that the objection of Mr. Weiner is well-founded, that you have gone straight in to simply putting to the witness that, "This is a forgery; who forged it?" You may, if you had wanted to, have put to him, "Isn't it the case that this was made out by somebody other than the hospital?" "Isn't it the case there's something wrong with the seal?" And learnt what, if anything, the witness could say about those matters. But it's a matter for the Tribunal in the end, of course, to determine whether or not all of the difficulties and deficiencies that you've carefully submitted demonstrate that the document is either a forgery or is unreliable and that we ought not to put any weight on it or that it's a document that we ought not even receive into evidence. I don't see, though, that most of those matters are things that you can effectively put to this witness in cross-examination. He will either -- well, he has told you where he has got the documents. There may, of course, be errors or mistakes in a document that have got nothing to do with this witness. They can be made by other people. They can be made genuinely or they can be made by fault, somebody trying to deceive. So those possibilities as to conclusion are for the Chamber. I think you have identified very clearly the matters that you want us to consider, whether or not the document might be regarded as a forgery or with suspicion. I don't think there's anything further you need to put to the witness about it, but if there is something, of course you might do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I accept your suggestions. Perhaps I rushed things a bit, but everything associated with this document is, believe me, a complex process. I should like to remind this distinguished Chamber that at the beginning of the examination of this witness, the Prosecutor asked the witness whether he was receiving any sort of emolument from the Croatian government, which he emphatically refused. Yesterday, when you asked Mr. Weiner and conveyed to him these discrepancies between the statements of the witness and this document, Mr. Weiner explained this to you, and I have to say to you that the three documents which were given to the Trial Chamber today under marks P86, 1, 2, and 3 were only subsequently submitted to us last night. So objectively the question arises - of course when I say this I try to have the whole picture in mind - if the witness brought these documents with him in The Hague, there is absolutely no reason for us to have been given this first finding only two days ago and what they presented to the Court today under P86 only last night. But that -- even that, only after you posed that particular question and observed this problem in connection with this particular document. That is what led me to express this opinion about that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Rodic. The record has recorded all those matters, and a number of them had been noted by the Chamber already. There will certainly be an issue of fact to be decided by the Chamber in due course about these matters. But if you have concluded that part of your questioning about the document, you may want to go on and finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should like to indicate in advance that perhaps I will be needing an extension of five to ten minutes in order for us to be able to complete this today, and I would like to ask your permission for that extension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've checked with the schedule. This courtroom won't be used until 3.30, according to the computer schedule, and so we would have no objection to finishing today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Move on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Needless to say, Your Honour, this also encompasses the question whether Colleague Weiner will be able of finishing his redirect today. If he could please let me have this information, because if he is, then I will give up a large portion of my own questions. I will certainly do my best to finish on my part, and that also begs the question of whether we will be able to discharge this witness, generally speaking, to leave The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We will finish today. I will do what's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would be grateful, then, if you could move on with every reasonable speed, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grbic [sic] the three documents, medical documents that were shown to you today, did you bring them together to The Hague with the one which was shown to us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not Grbic. I'm Mr. Vlasica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Mr. Vlasica.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second, I brought all the three documents, but to set your heart at rest, let me tell you, all these documents that I have also exist in the medical centre in Dubrovnik, identical documents. So you cannot put it to me that these are forgery. If there have been some mistakes made, this is their mistake, not my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know in what upper leg you were hurt?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do and how, because I can feel it quite acutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you intervene when you saw that it was written wrong if it is written wrong?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look here, the way Mr. Weiner put it and the way they recorded it, and of course what you are saying, what we are all claiming, when I stand in front of you, perhaps what is right to me is left to you. Maybe there was a confusion. Maybe they made a confusion. Maybe there was a mistake in the writing. But the facts are not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did the directrix herself write this down for you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she didn't. It was written by people who were in the surgical ward. Dr. Segedin, I believe it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wrote it and he took it to the lady director for her signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that the doctor -- and you claim that if the doctor is standing opposite you and is facing you, looking at you, he would write in his finding left leg because to him it is on the left, whereas in actual fact you had been wounded in the right leg; is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's for the doctors to state what the doctor would claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's well-founded, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's what the witness said to me, and then I asked him to confirm it. I'm not the one who put the question before he had explained it to me, rather. His explanation was the one that was given by Mr. Weiner, so now I'm asking him whether he is making the same assertion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? May I explain something, rather? As far as Segedin is concerned and the typing, Dr. Segedin did not write this in front of me. I asked for this two days in advance in order to get it out of my documentation from 1991 in terms of my wound, and I said that I had to bring it here. They wrote it out for me, and I just came to take this document. So Dr. Segedin did not see me himself at all. He just copied this from the documents that had to do with my medical treatment then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste any time. This is clear. Is it true, Mr. Vlasica, that in your statement there are some things that are simply missing? Your statement of the year 2000 there is not a single word about the platforms at certain -- on certain buildings that are cultural monuments in the Old Town. Also, there is no mention of big flags, UNESCO and Red Cross flags, that were flying on some buildings in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I'm going to mention all of this to you and then you will respond. Also, that in the morning of the 6th of December, you saw Tonci Skocko passing by your store and everything you said about him then. Also, there is no mention in your statement that you were surveying the damage sustained by the Old Town as you were being driven to hospital, and also that you -- your wound was sutured in hospital without any anaesthesia. Is that true, that none of these things that you did mention in your examination-in-chief is not part of the statement you gave to the investigators in 2000?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I told them about what they had asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Now let me ask you something else. When you talked to my distinguished friend Mr. Weiner on the 22nd, did you mention to him the mortar, Bogisica Park, the mortar in the park, the way in which it was fired, there was sporadic gunfire, that there was a lack of ammunition for the mortar in Bogisica Park, and also that they fired very little ammunition from Bogisica Park and that on the 6th of December, they ended their artillery support to the defenders at Srdj? Did you mention this to Mr. Weiner on the 22nd when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered the questions that Mr. Weiner had for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered you specifically. I have told you quite specifically, and I listened to you carefully, so I answered everything that he asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I want to get an accurate answer. All this information that I gave you just now -- please let me finish my question. All this information that I gave to you just now, everything I said to you just now about Bogisica Park, sporadic gunfire, the mortar, the lack of ammunition on the 6th of December, did you utter any of that? Did you tell Mr. Weiner about that?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Mr. Weiner about what he asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you did have knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was answering the questions that were being put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And you did not say a single word about this to the investigators in 2000?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you yet again, I told them about the things that they asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's not true. Your Honour, in 2000, if you look at the last paragraph of his statement, he states he's in the hospital, he's in the hospital with a person by the name of Zika, who was a soldier who was up on Srdj, part of the people defending Srdj, and they spoke about the war. He told him about the different things that happened and -- during that day. As a result, I asked him about that and he indicated. They didn't ask further, but there was discussion about Zika and all that information comes from Zika about what happened in Bogisica Park. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not agree with this objection, because in that part of the statement, in this last paragraph that my colleague read out, there is no mention whatsoever of Zika having said anything about Bogisica Park. The witness confirmed to me just now that he told Mr. Weiner about what he knew about Bogisica Park when they were preparing for this testimony, during the proofing. And if you remember, before the break I showed the photograph with the mortar in Bogisica Park, and I put questions in relation to that photograph. Then the witness denied it. Your Honour, in view of my promise, I would like to -- I beg your pardon. I thought that I was interrupting. I thought that you wished to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would like to complete the cross-examination of this witness by asserting, Mr. Vlasica, that you were not telling the truth before this Honourable Trial Chamber over these past two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I move the Trial Court to strike that. That's not a question, it was just an argument he made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, let me help Mr. Rodic and the record by asking the witness whether you agree with that proposition, that you were not telling the truth in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I came here, I took a solemn oath that I would speak the truth and nothing but the truth. What I said was the truth. And as for what Mr. Rodic said about me, I can only say thank you to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No re-direct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am pleased to be able to tell you that your evidence is now at an end and you are now free to return to your home. Thank you for your attendance and for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may leave the court, if you wish, now. And while you're going, could I mention to counsel that it seems in view of developments and the note that I have received during the morning, that it is convenient now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- as I understand it, for there to be no sitting on Monday as well as Tuesday. The reason for this is that, following the concern raised by the Prosecution the day before yesterday about the slow progress with medical testing and the concern echoed by Mr. Petrovic that this was simply taking too long to resolve, the question of the accused's health, I have been told that it has been possible to schedule both the urological and the MRI testing for this Monday, the urological in the morning and the MRI in the afternoon. I think in view of that and the importance of resolving this question of the fitness of the accused, we should take advantage of those appointments, and for that reason not sit on Monday. We had already decided not to sit on Tuesday. This seems to fit in with the Prosecution's schedule because of its embarrassment that a witness it had programmed for next week is unable to attend, and it's been greatly facilitated, Mr. Rodic, by the speed with which you were able to conclude your cross-examination of this last witness. That will mean that your client doesn't have to come in here on Monday, and he can just be able to attend to the medical appointments that have been made. So for the reasons indicated, the Chamber will not sit on Monday or Tuesday, and the hearing will continue on Wednesday. Do you want to say something, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has been informed about this, that thanks to your intervention, the MRI was moved ten days ahead. Also in relation to all these other arrangements, it is a response to your intervention that all of this has been speeded up. So I simply wish to thank you on behalf of the Defence for your prompt reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender those documents now. However, we're -- since I believe there is going to be some argument, maybe we should wait until Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question of their admission will be further considered when we resume. It's clear that there's going to be quite some consideration needed. So that can be dealt with next week. I thank counsel for their comments, and we will adjourn now until Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of March, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.56 p.m.,
